topic: Introduction to Fire Insurance and Fire Hazards
t: General insurance business in India, including fire insurance, was nationalised under the General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, with effect from:
o: 1 September 1956
1 April 1973
1 January 1972
1 January 1973
e: GIBNA 1972 brought 107 insurers under the General Insurance Corporation of India and its four subsidiaries with effect from 1 January 1973; 1 September 1956 was the date of life insurance nationalisation.

topic: Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy – Coverage and Exclusions
t: A batch of timber being seasoned inside a kiln catches fire within the kiln due to excessive heat. Under the fire peril of the SFSP policy, loss to the timber is:
o: Covered in full
Covered subject to 5% excess
Excluded, since property undergoing any heating or drying process is not covered for the fire peril
Covered under the explosion peril
e: The fire peril excludes loss to property undergoing a heating or drying process; however, if the fire spread beyond the kiln, damage to other property would be covered.

topic: Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy – Coverage and Exclusions
t: A stray buffalo wanders into an insured godown and knocks down a stack of goods, damaging them. Under the SFSP policy this loss is:
o: Excluded as not being a fire peril
Covered under the impact damage peril, since the animal did not belong to the insured
Covered only under the burglary policy
Excluded as an Act of God
e: Impact damage covers impact by rail/road vehicles or animals not belonging to or under the control of the insured or his employees.

topic: Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy – Coverage and Exclusions
t: Which of the following perils is excluded from the basic SFSP policy and must be added by endorsement for additional premium?
o: Riot, strike and malicious damage
Bursting of water tanks
Aircraft damage
Earthquake and volcanic eruption
e: Earthquake (fire and shock) is excluded from the SFSP policy and available as an add-on; RSMD, bursting of tanks and aircraft damage are among the twelve named perils.

topic: Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy – Coverage and Exclusions
t: The excess under the SFSP policy applies:
o: To each and every loss separately
Once per policy year irrespective of the number of losses
Only to losses exceeding ₹1 lakh
Only to stocks, not to buildings
e: The excess is deducted from each and every loss; where several losses occur in a year, each attracts the excess separately.

topic: Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy – Coverage and Exclusions
t: Loss or damage caused by ionising radiation or contamination by radioactivity from nuclear fuel or nuclear waste is treated under the SFSP policy as:
o: A named peril
Covered under the explosion peril
A general exclusion
Covered subject to a 5% excess
e: Nuclear perils are excluded from all standard property policies because of their catastrophic potential; such exposures are handled through specialised nuclear pools.

topic: Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy – Coverage and Exclusions
t: A landslide damages an insured warehouse in a hill station and the loss is assessed at ₹5,00,000. After the SFSP policy excess, the amount payable is:
e: Subsidence and landslide are AOG perils with an excess of 5% of the claim amount subject to a minimum of ₹10,000; 5% of ₹5,00,000 is ₹25,000, leaving ₹4,75,000.

t: Which of the following statements about Declaration policies is correct?
o: They can be issued for short periods of 3 or 6 months
They are issued with a provisional premium of 50% of the annual premium
The sum insured may be reduced by the insured during the policy period
They are issued for a full period of 12 months and cannot be issued for short periods
e: Declaration policies are annual contracts; the provisional premium is 75% of the annual premium, the sum insured cannot be reduced mid-term, and short-period issue is not permitted.

topic: Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy – Coverage and Exclusions
t: A factory suffers flood damage assessed at ₹3,00,000 under an SFSP policy. Applying the standard policy excess for Act of God perils, the amount payable is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). For AOG perils (lightning, STFI, subsidence and landslide) the excess is 5% of the claim amount subject to a minimum of ₹10,000. 5% of ₹3,00,000 is ₹15,000, which exceeds the minimum, so ₹2,85,000 is payable.

t: A timber depot located at the edge of a reserved forest should, in addition to the SFSP policy, obtain the add-on cover for:
o: Bush fire
Missile testing
Forest fire
Leakage from sprinklers
e: Forest fire is excluded from the bush fire peril of the SFSP policy and must be added by endorsement where the risk is exposed to forest areas.

t: The add-on cover for 'deterioration of stocks in cold storage' under the fire policy typically responds when stocks deteriorate due to:
o: Any power failure from whatever cause
Failure of power supply following damage by an insured peril at the premises of the power station or the insured's own premises
Mechanical breakdown of the refrigeration plant
Contamination by refrigerant leakage
e: The fire add-on is tied to insured perils; deterioration following refrigeration machinery breakdown is covered under a separate deterioration of stocks policy attached to machinery breakdown.

t: A floater policy under the fire tariff can be issued to cover:
o: Buildings at several locations
Plant and machinery at several locations
Buildings and stocks together
Stocks at various specified locations under a single sum insured
e: Floater policies are available only for stocks, whose location varies; buildings and machinery are fixed and must be insured location-wise.

topic: Standard Products – Bharat Griha Raksha, Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha and Bharat Laghu Udyam Suraksha
t: Under Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha, start-up expenses after an insured loss are included in the base cover up to:
o: ₹1 lakh
₹5 lakh
5% of the claim amount
e: The product builds in start-up expenses up to ₹1 lakh, along with other in-built covers such as removal of debris and professional fees, which are add-ons under the SFSP policy.

topic: Standard Products – Bharat Griha Raksha, Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha and Bharat Laghu Udyam Suraksha
t: Under Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha, cash kept at the insured premises is automatically covered against the insured perils up to:
o: ₹5 lakh
₹1 lakh
Nil – money is excluded
e: The product includes specific contents such as money up to ₹50,000, deeds and documents up to ₹50,000, and employees' personal effects up to ₹15,000 per person, without separate declaration.

topic: Standard Products – Bharat Griha Raksha, Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha and Bharat Laghu Udyam Suraksha
t: A jewellery showroom with building, fixtures and stock valued at a total of ₹8 crore at one location seeks fire cover under the IRDAI standard products. The appropriate product is:
o: Bharat Griha Raksha
Bharat Laghu Udyam Suraksha
Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha
Industrial All Risks
e: Bharat Laghu Udyam Suraksha is designed for enterprises with value at risk above ₹5 crore and up to ₹50 crore; Sookshma is for up to ₹5 crore and Griha Raksha for homes.

t: The main purpose of the condition of average in a fire policy is to:
o: Reduce the premium for large risks
Allow the insurer to cancel underinsured policies
Share losses between several insurers
Discourage underinsurance by making the insured bear a proportionate share of any loss when the sum insured is less than the value at risk
e: Since fire premium is charged on the sum insured, underinsurance would let the insured pay less premium while recovering partial losses in full; average corrects this inequity.

t: An insurer pays a fire claim of ₹8 lakh and later recovers ₹10 lakh from the negligent third party through subrogation. The excess recovery of ₹2 lakh:
o: Belongs to the insured, since the insurer cannot recover more than it has paid
Is retained by the insurer as profit
Is shared equally between insurer and insured
Must be paid to IRDAI
e: Subrogation is a corollary of indemnity: the insurer is entitled only to recoup what it paid, and any surplus recovery belongs to the insured.

t: A trader's stock is destroyed by fire. Books show opening stock ₹20 lakh, purchases to the date of fire ₹50 lakh and sales ₹60 lakh at a uniform gross profit of 20% on sales. Salvage realised ₹2 lakh. The net stock loss is:
o: ₹20 lakh
₹22 lakh
₹8 lakh
₹10 lakh
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Cost of goods sold = ₹60 lakh × 80% = ₹48 lakh. Stock at date of fire = 20 + 50 − 48 = ₹22 lakh; less salvage ₹2 lakh gives a net loss of ₹20 lakh.

t: For the contribution condition of a fire policy to operate, the policies concerned must:
o: Be issued by the same insurer
Have identical sums insured
Cover the same subject matter, the same peril and the same interest, and be in force at the time of loss
Have been issued on the same date
e: Contribution applies only among policies that overlap in subject matter, peril and insurable interest; a landlord's and a tenant's policies on the same building do not contribute, as the interests differ.

t: A building worth ₹1 crore is insured for ₹40 lakh with Insurer A and ₹40 lakh with Insurer B. A fire causes a loss of ₹20 lakh. Ignoring excess, Insurer A pays:
o: ₹10 lakh
₹8 lakh
₹4 lakh
₹16 lakh
e: Total insurance is ₹80 lakh against value ₹1 crore, so average reduces the recoverable loss to ₹16 lakh; this is shared equally by the two insurers, so A pays ₹8 lakh.

t: An insured wishes to increase the sum insured on stocks mid-term as stock levels have risen. The correct procedure is:
o: Take a fresh policy for the additional amount from a different insurer
Wait until renewal, as mid-term changes are not allowed
Inform the insurer after the loss
Request an endorsement increasing the sum insured, paying additional premium pro-rata for the unexpired period
e: Mid-term increases in sum insured are effected by endorsement and attract pro-rata additional premium; declaration or escalation covers can be used where fluctuations are expected.

t: The annual premium on a risk is ₹10,000. For a policy required for 9 months, the premium under the short period scale is:
e: The short period scale charges 85% of the annual premium for a period of up to 9 months; beyond 9 months the full annual premium applies.

t: Stocks worth ₹75 lakh are insured at a rate of ₹0.80 per mille. The basic premium (before GST) is:
e: ₹75,00,000 ÷ 1,000 × 0.80 = ₹6,000. The per mille rate is applied per ₹1,000 of sum insured.

t: A single fire policy covers a factory at Pune and a godown at Nashik. For rating purposes:
o: The Pune rate applies to both locations
Each location is rated separately according to its own occupancy, construction and protection
The higher of the two rates applies to both locations with a 10% loading
An average of the two rates applies
e: A specified-location policy rates each risk on its own merits; the 'highest rate plus 10%' rule applies only to floater policies on stocks.

t: Under the All India Fire Tariff 2001, a captive power plant situated outside the compound of the factory it serves is rated under the section for:
o: Storage risks
Industrial/manufacturing risks
Dwellings, offices and shops
Utilities located outside the compounds of industrial/manufacturing risks
e: The tariff has a separate section for utilities such as power plants, water treatment and effluent plants that are outside industrial compounds; inside the compound they take the industrial rate.

t: A house is mortgaged to a housing finance company for ₹30 lakh while its value is ₹80 lakh. Which statement about insurable interest is correct?
o: Both the mortgagor and the mortgagee have insurable interest; the mortgagor for the full value and the mortgagee to the extent of the loan
Only the mortgagee has insurable interest until the loan is repaid
Only the mortgagor has insurable interest
Neither has insurable interest until the mortgage is registered
e: The owner (mortgagor) retains full interest in the property, while the lender has an interest limited to the outstanding debt; this is why the agreed bank clause is used.

t: In a fire policy document, the details of the insured, the property, the sum insured, the premium and the period of insurance are set out in the:
o: Preamble
Operative clause
Schedule
Attestation clause
e: The schedule individualises the standard printed policy; the operative clause states the insurer's promise and the attestation clause carries the signature of the authorised official.

t: A shop is insured for ₹50 lakh at a rate of ₹1.20 per mille. The total premium payable including GST at 18% is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Basic premium = 50,00,000 ÷ 1,000 × 1.20 = ₹6,000; GST at 18% = ₹1,080, giving a total of ₹7,080.

t: Indian general insurers are required to cede a fixed percentage of every fire policy to GIC Re as obligatory cession. For recent financial years this percentage has been:
e: The obligatory cession to the Indian reinsurer was reduced over the years and has been fixed at 4% of each policy since FY 2022-23; the balance is placed under treaties and facultative arrangements.

t: Which statement about assignment of a fire policy is correct?
o: A fire policy may be freely assigned like a marine policy
Assignment is automatic on sale of the property
Assignment is prohibited under all circumstances
A fire policy is a personal contract and can be assigned only with the consent of the insurer, usually by endorsement
e: Unlike marine cargo policies, fire policies are not freely assignable because the identity and moral hazard of the insured matter; transfer of interest without consent terminates cover.

t: Which statement correctly describes the status of a surveyor's report in a fire claim?
o: The report is advisory; the insurer takes the decision on liability and quantum and may seek clarifications or an additional report
The report is binding on both the insurer and the insured
The insured may reject the report and appoint another surveyor
The report must be approved by IRDAI before payment
e: The licensed surveyor assesses the loss independently, but the decision to admit or reject a claim rests with the insurer, which must record reasons if it departs from the report.

t: Part of an insured building is damaged by fire. On the indemnity basis the claim is assessed as:
o: The full sum insured on the building
Cost of rebuilding the entire building
Reasonable cost of repairing the damaged portion, less an allowance for betterment where new materials improve on the old
Market value of the whole building
e: Partial losses are settled at the cost of repair; any improvement in the property beyond its pre-loss condition (betterment) is deducted so that the insured is not placed in a better position.

t: Stock insured for ₹10 lakh is valued at ₹12.5 lakh at the time of a fire. The gross loss is ₹5 lakh and salvage is sold for ₹1 lakh. After average and the ₹10,000 policy excess, the amount payable is:
e: Net loss after salvage = ₹4 lakh. Average: ₹4 lakh × 10/12.5 = ₹3,20,000. Less excess ₹10,000 gives ₹3,10,000.

t: Under the IRDAI (Protection of Policyholders' Interests) Regulations 2024, the free-look period for a policy with a term of one year or more is:
o: 15 days
30 days
45 days
60 days
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). 30 days from receipt of the policy document, irrespective of the sales channel.

t: In a fire claim on a manufacturer's finished goods, the loss is normally valued at:
o: Selling price including profit
Selling price less trade discount
Replacement cost of raw materials only
Cost of production (materials, labour and overheads) at the time of loss
e: Finished goods are indemnified at their cost of manufacture, not at selling price; the lost profit element is recoverable only under a consequential loss policy.

t: A fire-damaged roof is replaced with a superior and more expensive roofing material at the insured's request. Under an indemnity (market value) basis of settlement, the additional cost of the improvement is:
o: Borne by the insured as betterment
Paid by the insurer as part of reinstatement
Shared equally between insurer and insured
Paid by the insurer if the sum insured is adequate
e: Indemnity restores the insured to the pre-loss position, no better; the extra cost of superior materials is betterment and is deducted from the claim.

topic: Consequential Loss Insurance – Principles and Concepts
t: Which of the following expenses varies directly with turnover and is therefore usually treated as an uninsured working expense under a CL policy?
o: Depreciation of plant
Directors' fees
Carriage outward and freight on goods sold
Interest on term loans
e: Freight, packing, purchases and bad debts rise and fall with sales; depreciation, directors' fees and interest continue regardless and are standing charges.

topic: Consequential Loss Insurance – Principles and Concepts
t: The purpose of the increased cost of working item in a consequential loss policy is to:
o: Cover the cost of repairing damaged machinery
Reimburse additional expenditure reasonably incurred to avoid or diminish the reduction in turnover during the indemnity period
Pay the wages of workers laid off
Cover the premium for the material damage policy
e: ICOW encourages the insured to mitigate the interruption, e.g. by working overtime or hiring premises; repair costs belong to the material damage policy.

topic: Consequential Loss Insurance – Principles and Concepts
t: 'Shortage in turnover' under a consequential loss policy is:
o: The difference between the sum insured and the turnover achieved
The decline in turnover compared with the previous policy year
The difference between turnover in the policy year and the financial year
The amount by which the turnover during the indemnity period falls short of the standard turnover, in consequence of the damage
e: Shortage is measured against the (trend-adjusted) standard turnover for the corresponding period, and only the part attributable to the damage is indemnified.

topic: Consequential Loss Insurance – Principles and Concepts
t: A company's last financial year shows: turnover ₹100 lakh, opening stock ₹15 lakh, closing stock ₹20 lakh and uninsured working expenses ₹65 lakh. On the difference basis, gross profit is:
o: ₹40 lakh
₹35 lakh
₹30 lakh
₹45 lakh
e: Gross profit = (turnover + closing stock) − (opening stock + uninsured working expenses) = (100 + 20) − (15 + 65) = ₹40 lakh.

topic: Consequential Loss Policy – Coverage, Specification and Extensions
t: A cement plant whose production can be measured in tonnes may arrange its consequential loss policy on the 'output basis', under which:
o: Loss is measured by wages lost
Loss is measured by the number of days the plant is shut
Shortage is measured in units of output rather than in money value of sales, with the rate of gross profit applied per unit
Only standing charges are insured
e: The output basis suits businesses with a homogeneous product and stock buffers, since output loss is immediate even if sales from stock continue; the turnover basis remains the norm.

topic: Consequential Loss Policy – Coverage, Specification and Extensions
t: A Machinery Loss of Profits (MLOP) policy differs from a consequential loss (fire) policy in that the interruption must result from:
o: Fire and special perils
Riot and strike
Non-availability of raw materials
An accident indemnifiable under the machinery breakdown or boiler explosion policy
e: MLOP follows the machinery breakdown material damage cover and is usually subject to a time excess; a CL (fire) policy follows the SFSP material damage cover.

topic: Consequential Loss Policy – Coverage, Specification and Extensions
t: Which statement about insuring wages under a consequential loss policy is correct?
o: Wages may be insured either as part of gross profit (as a standing charge) or as a separate item on the pro-rata or dual basis
Wages can never be insured under a CL policy
Wages are always covered at 100% throughout the indemnity period
Wages are covered only through the lay-off extension
e: Salaries of permanent staff are usually a standing charge within gross profit, while wages of workers may be insured separately on a basis reflecting how long the insured intends to retain them.

t: An Insurance Ombudsman can entertain a complaint where the value of the claim, including expenses, does not exceed:
o: ₹20 lakh
₹30 lakh
₹50 lakh
₹1 crore
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). The limit was raised to ₹50 lakh by the amended Insurance Ombudsman Rules.

t: A CL policy has a sum insured of ₹60 lakh and an indemnity period of 18 months. Gross profit on the adjusted annual turnover is ₹40 lakh. An assessed loss of ₹9 lakh is payable as:
o: ₹6 lakh
₹4.5 lakh
₹9 lakh
₹8 lakh
e: The required sum insured is ₹40 lakh × 18/12 = ₹60 lakh, which equals the actual sum insured, so no average applies and the full ₹9 lakh is paid.

t: A small fire damages a machine and the material damage claim of ₹8,000 is not paid because it falls within the ₹10,000 excess under the SFSP policy. The resulting interruption causes a gross profit loss of ₹3 lakh. Under the material damage proviso, the CL claim is:
o: Not payable, as no material damage claim was paid
Payable at 50%
Payable only if the excess is waived
Payable, since the proviso is satisfied where the material damage claim would have been paid but for the operation of an excess
e: The proviso expressly treats a material damage claim rejected solely because of an excess or deductible as satisfying the link between the two policies.

t: The sum insured under the business interruption section of an Industrial All Risks policy is normally based on:
o: Gross profit for the selected indemnity period, as under a CL policy
Turnover of the last financial year
Total value of plant and machinery
Net profit only
e: Section II of the IAR policy follows consequential loss principles, with gross profit (adjusted for indemnity periods over 12 months) as the sum insured and average applying.

t: The Industrial All Risks policy is intended for:
o: Residential housing societies
Shops and offices in commercial complexes
Industrial and manufacturing risks with large sums insured
Storage risks of traders only
e: IAR was designed for large manufacturing units with multiple exposures; dwellings, shops and offices are insured under SFSP or the standard products such as Bharat Griha Raksha.

t: A fire hydrant system installed at an industrial premises in accordance with the TAC Fire Protection Manual essentially comprises:
o: Portable extinguishers placed at every 15 metres
A dedicated water storage, fire pumps, a ring main of piping and hydrant outlets with hoses and branch pipes
Automatic smoke detectors connected to the fire brigade
Fire-resistant doors on all openings
e: A hydrant installation provides pressurised water for manual fire fighting; the manual specifies tank capacity, pump duty, pipe sizes and hydrant spacing, and compliance earns a tariff discount.

t: A fire detector that operates when the temperature in its vicinity rises faster than a set rate per minute, irrespective of the absolute temperature, is a:
o: Ionisation smoke detector
Photoelectric smoke detector
Fixed-temperature heat detector
Rate-of-rise heat detector
e: Rate-of-rise detectors respond to rapid temperature increase and suit areas where smoke detectors would give false alarms; fixed-temperature detectors operate only at a preset temperature.
